unit.title: Use and maintain hand and power tools for electrical work

summary: This unit teaches you to choose, check, use and look after the hand and power tools of the electrical trade. You will learn to strip, terminate and crimp conductors, cut, deburr and bend conduit, make fixings in block, metal and wood, and use drills and angle grinders safely. You will also learn to clean, maintain, store and keep track of tools, and to take faulty ones out of use.

blocks.p: An electrician's work is only as good as the tools used and the way they are used. A screwdriver that slips, a stripper that nicks the copper or a grinder without its guard can damage the installation and injure you. This unit is for Level 2 trainees. It covers the tools you will use every day to install accessories, conduit, boxes and boards, and how to keep them in good, safe condition. It builds on the basic electrical safety unit (EEMELS0011B): every tool in this kit is used on circuits that are isolated and proved dead.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan and choose tools
List the tools a task needs, choose the right tool and the right size, and check each one before use.
Use hand tools for cables
Strip sheath and insulation without damage, cut conductors cleanly, shape them, terminate them firmly and crimp lugs and ferrules.
Use hand tools for conduit and boxes
Measure, mark, level, cut, deburr and bend conduit; make holes in boxes; draw cables in; fix boxes and saddles.
Use power tools safely
Check the tool, lead and supply; fit bits and discs with the tool unplugged; use drills and grinders with the right PPE and grip.
Make fixings
Drill block, concrete, metal and wood with the right bit and setting, and choose the right plug, anchor or screw.
Maintain tools
Clean, dry, oil and sharpen tools; replace blades and discs; look after batteries; tag and report faulty tools.
Store and control tools
Store tools dry, secure and organised; carry them safely; count them before a board is closed; keep the work area tidy.

ul: Most Jamaican buildings have walls of **concrete block**, often plastered (rendered), and concrete floors and roofs. You will drill a lot of masonry and fix many boxes and saddles to it.
Cables are usually run in **PVC conduit**, often cast into concrete or set in the block walls, so you will cut, bend and join a lot of it.
Many portable tools sold in Jamaica are rated **110–120 V**, but outlets may be 110 V or 220 V. Always check a tool's rating plate against the supply.
Heat, humidity and sea air make steel tools rust quickly, especially near the coast. Clean and dry tools every day.
Tools are expensive and easily stolen. Keep them locked away when you are not using them.

blocks.note: Use tools only on circuits that have been isolated, locked off and proved dead. Insulated tools give extra protection if something goes wrong; they do **not** make live work safe.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Plan the tools for the job

flow: Read the job and break it into steps
List the tools and PPE for each step
Collect them and check each one
Set them out where they will not be knocked or tripped over
Check again as the job changes

blocks.p: Example: fitting a surface outlet box on a block wall needs a tape measure, pencil and spirit level to mark it; a drill with a masonry bit, wall plugs and screws to fix it; a knife or sheath stripper, side cutters and wire strippers to prepare the conductors; long-nose pliers to shape them; and an insulated screwdriver of the right size to terminate them.

ul: Use each tool only for the job it was made for. A screwdriver is not a chisel or a lever; pliers are not a spanner; a spanner is not a hammer.
Use the **right size**: a screwdriver tip that fills the screw head, a spanner that fits the nut exactly.
Check the tool before use. Do not use a damaged tool; tag it and report it.
Never 'make do' with a tool that is too small or worn. Get the right one.
Keep tools clean and dry, and your hands free of grease, so tools do not slip.

head: PPE
When
rows: Safety glasses
Always when cutting, stripping, drilling, grinding, chiselling or working overhead
Face shield over safety glasses
Grinding and cutting with an angle grinder
Dust mask
Drilling or chasing block and concrete, cutting and sanding
Ear protection
Hammer drilling, grinding, chasing walls
Work gloves
Handling conduit, metal boxes and sharp edges; not when they could be caught by a turning drill
Safety boots
On site, always
Close-fitting clothes, hair tied back, no jewellery
Always near turning tools: chucks, bits and discs catch loose items

sections.title: Hand tools for cables and terminations

head: Tool
Used for
Watch out
rows: Flat (slotted) screwdriver
Slotted screws, terminal screws
Tip must fill the slot in width and thickness, or it slips and damages the screw
Cross-head screwdriver (Phillips, Pozidriv)
Cross-slot screws in accessories, boxes and fittings
Phillips and Pozidriv look alike but differ; the wrong one slips out ('cams out') and chews the head
Square-drive (Robertson) screwdriver
Square-hole screws, common on North American accessories
Match the size (often numbered 1, 2, 3)
Insulated screwdrivers and pliers
All terminal work
Marked 1000 V with a double triangle symbol; check the insulation before use
Torque screwdriver
Tightening terminals to the value in the maker's instructions
Set the value in N·m; it must be kept in calibration
Combination pliers
Gripping, twisting and bending conductors; cutting small wire
Not for nuts: the jaws slip and round the corners
Long-nose pliers
Shaping conductors and reaching into boxes
Do not twist heavy wire with the thin tips
Side cutters (diagonal cutters)
Cutting small conductors cleanly and flush
Do not cut hardened steel wire or screws with them
Cable cutters
Cutting larger cables cleanly without crushing
Choose cutters rated for the cable size
Wire strippers
Removing insulation from conductor ends
Set to the conductor size, or use the correct hole, so the copper is not nicked
Cable knife or sheath stripper
Removing the outer sheath of a cable
Cut away from your body; shallow cuts only, so the inner insulation is not damaged
Crimping tool (ratchet type)
Fixing lugs, terminals and ferrules onto conductor ends
Use the die that matches the terminal; the ratchet does not release until the crimp is complete
Hex (Allen) keys
Screws with a six-sided hole, such as some terminal and fixing screws
Use the exact size; worn keys round off the screw
Spanners and nut drivers
Nuts on glands, earth bars and fixings
Exact size; pull rather than push; never extend with a pipe

flow: Check the circuit is isolated and proved dead
Remove the outer sheath (if any) with a shallow cut, cutting away from you
Set the strippers to the conductor size, or choose the matching hole
Strip only the length the terminal needs: many accessories have a strip gauge moulded on the back
Look at the copper: no nicks, rings or cut strands
If the copper is damaged, cut it off and strip again

blocks.p: A **nick** is a ring cut into the copper. It makes the conductor thinner at that point, so it can break when it is bent, and it can overheat under load. The usual cause is strippers set too small for the conductor, or a knife used to strip insulation.

blocks.note: In Jamaica conductor sizes are usually given in **AWG**. The **smaller** the AWG number, the **thicker** the conductor: 12 AWG is thicker than 14 AWG. Strippers set for 14 AWG will close too far on a 12 AWG conductor and nick it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Screw-under terminals** (wrapped round a screw): form a loop with long-nose pliers and fit it **clockwise**, the way the screw tightens, so tightening pulls the loop in instead of pushing it out.
**Pillar or clamp terminals** (conductor pushed into a hole): insert the bare copper fully so no insulation is under the screw and no bare copper shows outside the terminal.
Do not cut strands off a stranded conductor to make it fit. Use a ferrule or the right terminal.
Tighten firmly with a screwdriver that fits, or to the torque the maker gives. A loose terminal overheats and can start a fire; an over-tightened one can crack the accessory or cut the conductor.
**Give each conductor a gentle pull** after tightening to check it is held.

flow: Choose the terminal or ferrule for the conductor size
Strip to the length of the terminal barrel
Insert the conductor fully into the barrel
Place it in the matching die of the crimping tool
Squeeze until the ratchet releases
Pull-test the crimp and check that no strands are outside the barrel

head: Insulated terminal colour
Conductor size (usual)
rows: Red
0.5 to 1.5 mm² (about 22 to 16 AWG)
Blue
1.5 to 2.5 mm² (about 16 to 14 AWG)
Yellow
4 to 6 mm² (about 12 to 10 AWG)

blocks.p: Always check the range printed on the packet: makers differ slightly. A terminal that is too big will not grip; one that is too small will not take all the strands.

sections.title: Hand tools for conduit, boxes and fixings

head: Tool
Used for
rows: Steel tape measure
Measuring box heights, conduit lengths and room sizes
Spirit level
Setting boxes, saddles, conduit and trunking level (horizontal) or plumb (vertical)
Try square or combination square
Marking a square cut line on conduit or trunking
Chalk line
Marking a long straight line on a wall or ceiling for a conduit run
Plumb line
Marking a true vertical line
Pencil or marker
Marking positions and cut lines
Centre punch
Making a small dent in metal, with a hammer, so a drill bit starts in the right place
Bradawl
Making a small starter hole in wood for a screw

head: Tool
Used for
Watch out
rows: Hacksaw
Cutting PVC and metal conduit, trunking and strut
Teeth point **away from the handle** so it cuts on the push stroke; blade tensioned with the wing nut
Junior hacksaw
Small cuts in tight places
Light work only
Ratchet conduit cutter
Cutting PVC conduit cleanly by squeezing the handles
Keep the blade sharp; rotate as you cut on larger sizes
Reamer, file or deburring tool
Removing burrs from inside and outside the cut end
Burrs cut cable insulation when cables are pulled in
Bending spring
Bending light PVC conduit by hand without kinking
Must match the conduit size; tie a cord to it to pull it out
Heat gun
Softening heavier PVC conduit for bending
Hot: keep it moving and away from your skin and anything that burns; follow your instructor
Hand bender
Bending steel conduit
Use the bender made for that conduit size
Fish tape (draw wire)
Pulling conductors through conduit
Tape the conductors on smoothly so the joint does not snag
Knockout punch, step drill, hole saw
Making clean round holes in metal boxes and enclosures
Drill a pilot hole first; deburr afterwards

blocks.p: Blades are graded in teeth per inch (TPI). Thin material needs fine teeth, because **at least three teeth should be touching the material** at once, or the teeth catch and break. Use a fine blade (about 24 or 32 TPI) for thin-walled conduit and trunking, and a coarser blade (about 18 TPI) for thicker metal. Use steady, full-length strokes, pressing only on the forward stroke.

blocks.h: Cutting, deburring and bending PVC conduit

flow: Measure the length and mark the cut line all round the conduit, so the cut will be square
Hold the conduit in a vice or on a bench hook, without crushing it
Cut on the mark with a fine-tooth hacksaw or a conduit cutter
Remove the burrs from inside and outside the end
For a bend: push in a bending spring of the right size, on a cord, until its middle is at the bend
Bend slowly over your knee or a former, a little past the angle you want, then ease it back
Twist and pull the spring out with the cord, and check the bend with a square

blocks.note: PVC bends more easily in Jamaica's warm weather than in a cold room, but a bend made too quickly or too tightly will still flatten or kink. A kinked conduit makes cables hard to pull and can damage their insulation: cut it out and make the bend again.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Push the fish tape through from one box to the next
Strip the conductor ends, hook them through the tape's eye and bind the joint smoothly with tape
One person feeds the conductors in straight, without kinks; the other pulls steadily
Use cable-pulling lubricant made for the job on long runs
Leave enough spare conductor at each box for terminating

head: Tool
Used for
Watch out
rows: Cold chisel
Cutting chases (grooves) in block for conduit and boxes, and cutting off bolts
Keep the head free of 'mushrooming'; wear safety glasses
Plugging chisel and bolster
Cutting out mortar joints; cutting block and brick
Hold with a hand guard if you have one
Club (lump) hammer
Striking chisels and bolsters
Use a hammer that suits the chisel
Claw hammer
Driving nails and pulling them out with the claw
Not for striking chisels
Ball pein hammer
Striking a centre punch and metalwork
Check the head is tight on the handle

blocks.note: Before cutting a chase in a wall, check for hidden cables and pipes, and ask your supervisor how deep and where the chase may go. A deep chase, especially across a wall, can weaken it.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Power tools: supply, checks and safe use

ul: **Voltage**: the tool's rating plate must match the outlet. A 110–120 V tool on 220 V gets about twice its rated voltage and can burn out or catch fire at once.
**GFCI (RCD) protection**: on site, and anywhere damp or outdoors, use a GFCI-protected outlet or plug a portable GFCI into the outlet first. Press its TEST button before you start.

**Extension leads**: rated for the tool's current, made for site or outdoor use, and **fully unwound** from the drum when a tool will run for a long time. A coiled lead cannot lose its heat and can melt.
**Battery tools** are often the best choice: no lead to trip over, cut or get wet, and no shock risk from a damaged lead.

head: Tool
How it is protected
Check
rows: **Double-insulated (Class II)**: marked with a square inside a square
Two layers of insulation, so the case should not become live; no earth (ground) conductor needed
Two-pin plug is normal; case must not be cracked
**Earthed (Class I)**: usually a metal case and a three-pin plug
The earth pin carries fault current so the breaker trips if the case becomes live
The earth pin must be present and undamaged; never cut it off or use an adaptor that leaves it unconnected

head: Part
Look for
rows: Plug
Cracks, burn marks, bent or loose pins, a missing earth pin
Lead
Cuts, crushing, kinks, tape repairs; the outer sheath gripped where it enters the plug and the tool
Case
Cracks, missing screws, signs of overheating
Switch
Moves freely, switches off properly, does not stick on
Guards and handles
Fitted, secure and working; side handle available
Chuck, bit, blade or disc
Undamaged, sharp, the right type, fitted tightly
Inspection label
Where the Centre uses them: inspected, and the next test date not passed

ul: **Unplug** the tool (or remove the battery) before changing a bit, blade or disc, cleaning it or making an adjustment.
Remove the **chuck key** before switching on. A key left in the chuck is thrown out at speed.
Check the switch is off before plugging in.
Hold the tool firmly with both hands, using the side handle on large drills and all grinders. If a bit jams, the tool twists hard; the side handle lets you hold it.
Let the tool do the work. Pushing too hard overheats the motor and the bit, and can snap the bit.
Keep the lead behind you and away from the bit, blade or disc.
Clamp small or loose work; never hold it in your hand or on your knee.
Tie back long hair, keep sleeves close and remove jewellery: a turning chuck winds them in.
Never carry a tool by its lead or unplug it by pulling the lead.
Wait for the tool to stop before putting it down.

blocks.h: If a tool sparks, smokes or smells of burning

flow: Switch off at once
Unplug it (or remove the battery)
Tag it 'DO NOT USE' with the fault, date and your name
Put it where nobody will pick it up
Report it

head: Drill
Best for
rows: Cordless drill/driver
Small holes in wood and metal, driving screws, work on ladders and in ceilings
Combi (hammer) drill, corded or cordless
General drilling, with a hammer setting for block and brick
Rotary hammer (SDS)
Heavy drilling in concrete and block; uses special SDS bits; some can chisel
Impact driver
Driving long screws and bolts; not for drilling large holes

head: Bit
Material
Setting
rows: Masonry bit (tungsten carbide tip)
Block, brick, concrete, plaster
Hammer on
High-speed steel (HSS) twist bit
Steel, aluminium, plastic, and wood
Hammer off
Spade (flat) bit
Large holes through timber joists and studs
Hammer off; steady speed
Hole saw (with pilot bit)
Large round holes: downlights in ceiling board, entries in boxes
Hammer off; slow speed
Step drill
Clean round holes in thin sheet metal boxes and trunking
Hammer off; slow speed
Tile bit
Ceramic tiles before drilling the wall behind
Hammer off until through the tile

blocks.p: **Speed**: the bigger the bit, the slower the speed. Drill metal slowly, with a drop of cutting oil, to keep the bit sharp. The hammer setting is only for masonry: it damages metal bits and splits wood and tiles.

blocks.h: Drilling a block wall for fixings

flow: Check the wall for hidden cables and pipes with a detector, and look for boxes and switches nearby
Mark the hole and check the plug packet for the bit size and depth
Put on safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection
With the drill unplugged, fit the masonry bit firmly; remove the chuck key; fit the side handle and the depth stop
Set hammer action; hold the drill square to the wall with both hands
Start slowly so the bit does not wander, then let the drill do the work
Pull the bit back now and then to clear the dust
Unplug the drill, let the bit cool, clean out the hole and push in the plug

blocks.note: Cables and conduits usually run straight up, down or across from switches, outlets and boards. **Do not drill in line with them.** A cable detector helps, but it can miss cables deep in concrete or inside metal conduit, so treat it as a guide, not a guarantee. If you hit something unexpected, stop and tell your supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Centre punch the hole position
Clamp the work or the box firmly
Drill a small pilot hole
Open it up with a larger bit, step drill, hole saw or knockout punch
Deburr the hole
Clear away the sharp swarf with a brush, not your fingers

head: Fixing
Use
Tips
rows: Plastic wall plug and screw
Boxes, saddles and fittings on solid block, brick and concrete
Use the bit size printed on the packet; hole slightly deeper than the plug; plug flush with the surface
Hammer-in (nail) plug
Quick fixing of saddles and clips in masonry
Light loads only
Sleeve anchor or concrete screw
Heavier items such as boards and steel strut
Follow the maker's hole size and depth
Cavity fixing (spring toggle, hollow-wall anchor)
Hollow ceiling board, drywall and hollow parts of blocks
Choose one rated for the load
Self-drilling metal screws
Fixing to steel strut and thin steel
Use a driver with the right bit; do not over-tighten
Wood screws
Timber, with a pilot hole made by a bradawl or small bit
Pilot hole stops the wood splitting

ul: A bit **too big** for the plug lets the plug spin in the hole, and the screw never tightens.
A bit **too small** makes the plug hard to push in and it may split the plaster or crush.
The screw must be long enough to pass through the item and the full length of the plug, so the plug opens out and grips.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican walls are built of **hollow concrete blocks**. A hole can break through into a hollow core, and an ordinary plug will then just spin. Move the fixing to a solid part of the block, use a fixing made for hollow walls, or use the method your instructor shows.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Angle grinders and other cutting tools

blocks.p: An angle grinder spins a disc at around 10,000 rpm or more. It cuts steel strut, threaded rod, conduit and slots in enclosures quickly, but a broken disc or a kickback can cause terrible injuries. Use it only after training, and only when no safer tool will do.

head: Check
Why
rows: The disc's maximum speed (rpm), printed on it, is at least the grinder's no-load speed
A disc run faster than its rating can burst
The disc's diameter and hole size match the grinder
A larger disc will not fit under the guard and may run too fast at its rim
The right type: thin cutting disc for cutting; thicker grinding disc for grinding; diamond disc for masonry
Using the flat face of a thin cutting disc to grind can shatter it
No cracks, chips or damp; not past any expiry date marked on its centre ring
A damaged or old disc can break apart in use
Fitted with the grinder unplugged, using the proper flange and key
Prevents the grinder starting while your hand is on the disc

flow: Check the grinder, lead and plug; the guard fitted and set between you and the disc
Wear safety glasses with a face shield, ear protection, gloves and close-fitting clothes
Clear away anything that can burn, and have an extinguisher ready: sparks travel several metres
Clamp the work firmly; never hold it in your hand
Hold the grinder with both hands, using the side handle
Start it and let it reach full speed before it touches the work; run a new disc for about a minute first, away from people
Stand to one side, never in line with the disc
Cut steadily without forcing or twisting the disc
Switch off and wait for the disc to stop before putting the grinder down; then unplug it

blocks.note: **Never use a grinder with the guard removed.** If a grinder's guard is missing or damaged, the grinder is unsafe: do not use it, tag it and report it. A face shield does not replace the guard.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: After hot work, such as grinding or cutting metal, check the area for smouldering material for some time afterwards. Dry grass, sawdust, cardboard and cable packaging catch fire easily in the dry season.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Tool
Use
Safety points
rows: Wall chaser
Cutting two parallel slots in block or plaster for a chase
Very dusty: use dust extraction, a dust mask and glasses; check for cables first
Jigsaw
Cutting openings in ceiling board and sheet material
Check what is behind the cut; keep fingers clear of the blade
Reciprocating saw
Rough cutting of timber, pipe and strut
Hold firmly with both hands; check behind the cut
Heat gun
Bending heavy PVC conduit, shrinking heat-shrink sleeves
The nozzle stays hot after use: rest it on its stand, away from anything that burns

blocks.p: Well-kept tools work better, last longer and are safer. Look after them at the end of every job, and inspect the whole kit regularly, recording the checks.

head: Tool
Care
rows: All hand tools
Wipe off dust, plaster and grease with a dry cloth after use. Dry them if wet, so they do not rust.
Pliers and cutters
A drop of light oil on the joint; work them open and shut; wipe off the extra so the handles are not slippery. Check the cutting edges meet.
Screwdrivers
Check the tip is not worn, rounded, chipped or twisted. A worn tip slips: replace the screwdriver.
Insulated tools
Check the insulation for cracks, cuts, burns or bare metal. A damaged insulated tool is replaced, **never taped or painted**.
Hacksaws and knives
Replace blunt blades and blades with missing teeth; fit hacksaw blades teeth forward and tension them.
Chisels and punches
Have a 'mushroomed' head ground back to shape by someone trained to do it; keep the cutting edge sharp.
Hammers
Check the head is tight; replace a cracked or split handle.
Files
Always fit a handle; clean the teeth with a file card (wire brush).
Tape measures and levels
Wipe the tape before winding it in; check the level's bubble vials are not cracked.

ul: Unplug the tool, then brush the dust out of the vents so the motor stays cool.
Keep the chuck clean; check bits and discs for wear and replace them.
Check the lead, plug and case as in the pre-use check.
Repairs to the motor, switch, lead or plug are done only by someone trained and authorised. Never tape a damaged lead.
Charge a battery only on **its own charger**, as the maker says.
Do not leave batteries in a hot vehicle or in the sun: heat shortens their life and can make them dangerous.
Modern lithium-ion batteries do **not** need to be run flat before charging.
Store them cool and dry, away from metal objects such as screws, coins and keys that could short the terminals.
A battery that is **swollen, cracked, leaking or very hot** must not be used or charged. Keep it away from anything that burns, and report it for safe disposal.

blocks.h: Taking a tool out of use

flow: Stop using it
Unplug it or remove the battery
Fix a 'DO NOT USE' tag: the fault, the date, your name
Put it apart from the good tools
Record it on the tool register and report it

blocks.p: A **tool register** (or inspection log) lists each tool, the date it was checked, its condition, and anything done to it. It shows what is fit for use, what is waiting for repair, and what is missing.

head: Item
Store it
rows: Hand tools
Clean and dry, in a lockable toolbox or on a tool board with a place for each one
Drill bits and hole saws
In a case or holder with a slot for each size, so edges do not chip against each other
Power tools
In their own cases, or on shelves in a dry, lockable store
Leads and extension drums
Coiled loosely without kinks, hung up or put away; drums wound in when stored; kept out of the sun
Batteries
Cool, dry, away from metal objects; never in a hot vehicle
Faulty tools
Tagged, apart from the good tools, until repaired or thrown away

ul: Carry tools in a tool belt, pouch or bag, not in your trouser pockets: sharp points and blades can cut or stab you when you bend, kneel or fall.
Pass a tool to someone handle first.
On a ladder, keep both hands free to climb. Use a tool belt, or raise and lower tools in a bucket or bag on a line. Never throw tools up or down.
Do not leave tools on the top of a ladder or on a scaffold edge where they can fall.

blocks.p: A tool left inside a board, a ceiling or a box can cause a short circuit, an arc flash or damage when the supply is restored. Use a toolbox or tool board with a place for each tool, or a tool list, and **count your tools at the end of each task and before any board is closed or switched on**. Report a missing tool at once.

ul: Keep leads out of walkways and coil them away when not in use.
Sweep up off-cuts, stripped insulation, swarf, screws and dust as you go, so nobody slips or trips.
Put waste in the right bins: copper and metal scrap apart (it can be recycled), PVC and packaging apart.
Old lamps, especially fluorescent tubes and compact fluorescent lamps, contain mercury: do not break them; keep them apart for safe disposal as the Centre's rules say.
Never leave off-cuts in ceiling spaces, drains or the customer's bins without permission.
At the end of the day, clean the tools, lock them away and report anything lost or damaged.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can list the tools and PPE a task needs and check each tool before use.
I can choose the right screwdriver, pliers, cutters and strippers for a task, and say what each is for.
I can strip a conductor without nicking it and explain why a nick is dangerous.
I can terminate conductors firmly, looping them clockwise under a screw, and pull-test them.
I can crimp a terminal using the right size and die.
I can measure, mark, cut, deburr and bend PVC conduit, and fit a hacksaw blade correctly.
I can make holes in metal boxes and draw cables into conduit.
I can check a power tool, its lead and its supply, and explain double insulation and earthed tools.
I can choose the right drill, bit, speed and setting for block, metal and wood.
I can drill a block wall safely and choose the right plug or anchor, including for hollow blocks.
I can choose and fit an angle grinder disc and use the grinder safely.
I can clean, oil and maintain hand tools and look after cordless batteries.
I can tag and report a faulty tool and record it on the tool register.
I can store and carry tools safely, count them before a board is closed, and keep the area tidy.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: 1000 V and a double triangle
Marking on insulated hand tools
At least 3 teeth
Hacksaw teeth in contact with the material
About 24 or 32 TPI
Fine hacksaw blade for thin-walled conduit
Red / blue / yellow
Crimp terminals for about 0.5–1.5 / 1.5–2.5 / 4–6 mm²
12 AWG is thicker than 14 AWG
Lower AWG number, thicker conductor
Disc rpm ≥ grinder rpm
Rule for grinder discs
About 5 mA
Trip level of a GFCI that protects people
Square inside a square
Double-insulated (Class II) tool

terms: Bending spring
A steel spring pushed inside PVC conduit to stop it kinking while it is bent by hand.
Burr
A sharp, rough edge left on metal or plastic after cutting.
Chase
A groove cut in a wall to take a conduit or cable.
Chuck
The part of a drill that grips the bit; a keyed chuck is tightened with a chuck key.
Crimping
Squeezing a terminal or ferrule onto a conductor with a crimping tool so it grips permanently.
Double insulation (Class II)
Two layers of insulation, shown by a square inside a square, so the tool needs no earth conductor.
Fish tape (draw wire)
A long flexible steel or nylon tape used to pull conductors through conduit.
GFCI / RCD
A device that cuts the supply when current leaks to earth, protecting people using power tools.
Insulated tool
A hand tool with insulated handles and shaft, tested and marked for use up to 1000 V.
Knockout punch
A tool that cuts a clean round hole in a metal box or enclosure.
Masonry bit
A drill bit with a hard tungsten carbide tip for block, brick and concrete.
Mushroomed head
The spread, ragged head of a chisel or punch after much striking; pieces can fly off.
Nick
A cut into the copper of a conductor, which weakens it.
Reamer
A tool for removing the burr from the inside of a cut conduit.
Strip gauge
A mark on an accessory that shows how much insulation to strip.
Swarf
Sharp chips and curls of metal made by drilling or cutting.
Tool register
A record of each tool, its checks, condition and any repairs.
TPI
Teeth per inch: how fine a saw blade is.
Wall plug
A plastic sleeve pushed into a drilled hole so a screw can grip in masonry.

c1.title: A new outlet in an Ironshore house
c1.text: Trainee Kadeem Morris is working with electrician Mr Peter Grant in a concrete-block house at Ironshore, St James. The circuit has been isolated, locked off and proved dead. They are fixing a surface box and fitting a new duplex outlet on 12 AWG copper conductors. The outlet has screw terminals and a strip gauge moulded on the back. Kadeem's adjustable wire strippers are still set from an earlier job on 14 AWG conductors.

c2.title: A conduit run in an Annotto Bay shop
c2.text: Trainee Shantel Reid and electrician Mr Errol Gayle are running 20 mm PVC conduit on the surface of a shop wall in Annotto Bay, St Mary, from a switch to a steel trunking above the counter. The run needs one 90° bend. Shantel will cut the conduit with a hacksaw, bend it with a bending spring, make an entry in the steel trunking and pull the conductors in with a fish tape.

c3.title: Fixing a board at a Porus clinic
c3.text: Trainee Lenworth Campbell and his supervisor Mrs Maxine Ellis are fixing a new distribution board and conduit saddles to a plastered wall of hollow concrete blocks at a clinic in Porus, Manchester. A light switch is already fitted on the same wall. They have a corded 110 V hammer drill, a 30 m extension drum, masonry bits and a box of plastic wall plugs.

c4.title: Cutting steel at a Bull Bay pumping station
c4.text: At a water pumping station near Bull Bay, St Andrew, trainee Andre Thomas must cut lengths of steel strut channel with a 115 mm angle grinder marked 'no-load speed 11,000 rpm'. The disc bucket holds a cutting disc marked 'max 8,500 rpm' and another marked 'max 13,300 rpm'. The grinder's guard is not on the tool. The work is just inside the doorway of the pump house, and the grass outside is dry.

c5.title: Friday tool check in Claremont
c5.text: On Friday afternoon, trainees at a training centre in Claremont, St Ann, inspect the workshop's electrical toolkit and record their findings on the tool register. They find an insulated screwdriver with a crack in its handle insulation near the shaft, a cold chisel whose head has spread out into a ragged rim, and a cordless drill battery that has swollen so it no longer clicks into the drill.

questions.q: Kadeem uses his strippers, still set for 14 AWG, on the 12 AWG conductors. What is most likely to happen?
o: The blades will not reach the insulation, so it stays on
The blades will close too far and nick the thicker copper
The conductors will strip cleanly, as the sizes are so close
The conductor will be stripped too long for the terminal
questions.why: A lower AWG number means a thicker conductor, so 12 AWG is thicker than 14 AWG. Blades set for the thinner size close too far and cut into the copper. Always set the strippers, or choose the hole, for the conductor you are stripping.

questions.q: How much insulation should Kadeem strip from each conductor for the outlet?
o: About 50 mm, so there is spare copper to trim off later
As little as possible, leaving some insulation under the screw
Enough to wrap the copper twice around each terminal screw
The length shown by the strip gauge on the back of the outlet
questions.why: The strip gauge shows exactly how much bare copper the terminal needs. Too much leaves bare copper showing outside the terminal; too little puts insulation under the screw, giving a poor connection that can overheat.

questions.q: Kadeem has tightened all the terminal screws. Which final check shows that each conductor is properly held?
o: A gentle pull on each conductor to see it does not move
A tap on each terminal screw with the screwdriver handle
Bending each conductor back and forth to test its strength
Switching the circuit on to see whether the outlet works
questions.why: A gentle pull shows a conductor is gripped by its terminal. Bending conductors back and forth weakens the copper, and switching on is not a check of the terminations: a loose one may work at first and overheat later.

questions.q: The wall plug packet says 'use a 6 mm bit', but Kadeem has only a 7 mm masonry bit with him. What is likely to happen if he uses it?
o: The plug will be hard to push in and will split the plaster
The plug will spin in the hole and the screw will not tighten
The fixing will be stronger, as the plug has more room to open
The bit will break, as 7 mm bits are too big for hammer drilling
questions.why: A plug needs a hole of the size on the packet so that it is gripped tightly and opens out as the screw goes in. In an oversized hole it turns with the screw and never grips. Use the right bit, or the right size of plug for the bit.

questions.q: Shantel's hacksaw skids on the conduit and hardly cuts on the forward stroke. She sees the teeth point towards the handle. What should she do?
o: Press down harder on the back stroke so the saw cuts that way
Loosen the wing nut so the blade can flex more as she saws
Refit the blade with its teeth facing forward and tension it
Saw much faster with short strokes until the blade starts to bite
questions.why: A hacksaw is made to cut on the push stroke, so the teeth must point away from the handle. Refit the blade that way and tighten the wing nut until the blade is taut. A loose blade wanders and can snap.

questions.q: Which hacksaw blade is best for cutting the thin-walled 20 mm conduit?
o: A fine blade, so at least three teeth touch the thin wall
A coarse blade, so it cuts through the wall more quickly
A blade with teeth on both edges, used back and forth
A wood saw blade, since PVC is a soft material much like wood
questions.why: At least three teeth should be in contact with the material. On a thin wall, coarse teeth straddle it, catch and break. A fine blade, about 24 or 32 teeth per inch, gives a clean cut.

questions.q: Shantel must make a 20 mm hole in the side of the steel trunking for the conduit connector. Which method gives the cleanest hole?
o: A 20 mm masonry bit with the hammer setting turned on
A cold chisel and club hammer, then finish with a file
A 20 mm spade bit run at the drill's highest speed
A pilot hole, then a step drill or a knockout punch
questions.why: A step drill or a knockout punch, started from a pilot hole, makes a clean round hole in thin sheet steel. Masonry and spade bits are for other materials and tear thin metal; a chisel leaves a ragged hole. Deburr the hole afterwards.

questions.q: How should Shantel attach the conductors to the fish tape before pulling them in?
o: Tie the conductors in a large knot round the end of the tape
Hook the stripped ends through the eye and tape them smoothly
Hold them beside the tape and push both into the conduit
Push the conductors in first, then push the fish tape after them
questions.why: Hooking the stripped ends through the eye and binding the joint smoothly makes a slim, firm head that will not snag on the bend or the conduit ends. A big knot jams, and conductors pushed on their own buckle and kink.

questions.q: Where on the wall is Lenworth most likely to hit a hidden conduit if he drills?
o: Straight above or below the light switch
In the middle of a bare wall, far from any box
In a mortar joint between two of the blocks
Beside the window, well away from any switch
questions.why: Conduits and cables usually run straight up, down or across from switches, outlets and boards. Drilling in line with an accessory is the commonest way to hit a hidden cable. Check with a detector, but remember it can miss some cables.

questions.q: The hammer drill will run on the 30 m extension drum for about an hour. How should the drum be used?
o: Unwind only what is needed, so less lead lies on the floor
Leave it wound and plug the drill into the drum's outlet
Wind the lead tighter so the drum sits steady on the floor
Unwind the lead fully, so it cannot build up heat and melt
questions.why: A lead coiled on a drum cannot lose the heat made by the current, so under a long or heavy load it can overheat and melt. Unwind it fully, and run the spare lead safely out of the walkway.

questions.q: The masonry bit is getting very hot and the hole is hardly getting deeper. What should Lenworth do?
o: Push much harder on the drill so the bit bites into the block
Stop, let the bit cool, and pull it back often to clear the dust
Switch the drill to reverse so the dust is pushed out of the hole
Pour a little water into the hole while the drill is running
questions.why: Dust packed in the hole stops the bit cutting and makes it overheat. Let it cool, check it is sharp and the hammer action is on, and pull it back now and then to clear the dust. Forcing it can snap the bit; water near a mains drill risks a shock.

questions.q: One hole breaks through into the hollow core of a block, and the plug just spins. What should Lenworth do?
o: Pack paper into the hole and push the same plug back in
Fit a longer screw so it forces the plug tighter in the hole
Move to solid block, or use a fixing for hollow walls
Wrap the plug in insulating tape so it fits more tightly
questions.why: An ordinary plug needs solid material round it to grip. In a hollow core it has nothing to grip, and packing or a longer screw will not hold a board safely. Move the fixing to a solid part, or use a fixing made for hollow walls, as the instructor shows.

questions.q: Which disc may Andre fit to the grinder?
o: The one marked 8,500 rpm, as a slower disc is safer
Either disc, as long as the guard is fitted first
The one marked 13,300 rpm, if it is not damaged
Whichever disc is thicker, as it will be stronger
questions.why: A disc's maximum speed must be at least the grinder's no-load speed (11,000 rpm). The 8,500 rpm disc would be run faster than it is made for and could burst. Check the chosen disc for cracks and damage too.

questions.q: The grinder's guard is missing. What should happen?
o: Do not use it: tag it and report it until a guard is fitted
Use it carefully, holding the side handle with both hands
Use it, but wear a full face shield to make up for the guard
Use it for short cuts only, keeping the disc away from him
questions.why: The guard is there to stop pieces of a broken disc, and sparks, hitting the user. Nothing replaces it. A grinder without its guard must be taken out of use and reported.

questions.q: With a guard fitted, where should Andre stand while he cuts the strut?
o: Straight behind the disc, to see the cut line clearly
Facing the disc, with his chin just above the guard
Kneeling on the strut to hold it still while it is cut
To one side of the disc, out of line with its path
questions.why: If a disc breaks, the pieces fly out in line with the disc. Standing to one side keeps you out of that path. The strut must be clamped, never held still with a foot or knee.

questions.q: Sparks from the cuts will fly out of the doorway onto the dry grass. What should be done before Andre starts?
o: Close the door so the sparks stay inside the pump house
Clear or wet the area and keep an extinguisher close by
Cut quickly so that the grinder makes fewer sparks
Wear leather gloves so the sparks cannot cause harm
questions.why: Grinding sparks travel several metres and can set dry grass, paper and packaging alight. Clear or wet the area, have an extinguisher ready, and check for smouldering material for a while after the work.

questions.q: What should be done with the insulated screwdriver that has cracked insulation near the shaft?
o: Wrap the crack with insulating tape and keep using it
Keep it, but use it only on 110 V circuits from now on
Seal the crack with a little glue and carry on using it
Take it out of use and replace it with a new rated one
questions.why: Once its insulation is damaged, the tool no longer meets its 1000 V rating, and tape or glue cannot restore it. Tag it, record it on the register and replace it.

questions.q: Why must the cold chisel with the spread, ragged head be dealt with before it is used again?
o: Sharp pieces can break off the head and fly when it is struck
The spread head makes the chisel cut a wider and rougher chase
The ragged head stops the chisel from fitting in the toolbox
A spread head shows that the chisel is too soft to cut block
questions.why: Repeated hammering spreads the head into a 'mushroom'. When struck, sharp pieces can break off and fly into eyes or hands. Someone trained grinds the head back to shape; until then the chisel is not used.

questions.q: What should be done with the swollen cordless drill battery?
o: Charge it fully, which will bring it back to its normal shape
Push it firmly into the drill and use it until it runs flat
Stop using it, keep it cool and report it for disposal
Leave it on its charger overnight so the cells can balance out
questions.why: A swollen lithium-ion battery is damaged inside and can overheat or catch fire, especially when charged or forced. Do not use or charge it; keep it away from anything that burns and report it for safe disposal.

questions.q: Which colour of insulated crimp terminal usually suits a 2.5 mm² conductor?
o: Red
Blue
Yellow
Black
questions.why: The usual colour code is red for about 0.5–1.5 mm², blue for about 1.5–2.5 mm² and yellow for about 4–6 mm². Always check the range printed on the packet, as makers differ slightly.
